```{python}
#| label: setup
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _lib.orplot import new_axes, shade_polygon, convex_hull, mark_point, COLORS
from _lib.toy_ip import A, b, c, lp, ip_optimum, integer_points, all_rows, polygon, facility_location
```

## The idea

Drop the integrality requirement from an integer program and you get a linear program,
its **LP relaxation**. The relaxation is easy to solve and, for a maximization problem,
its value is an **upper bound** on the integer optimum, because it optimizes over a
larger set.

The relaxation depends on how the problem was written down. Many different systems of
inequalities have exactly the same integer solutions, but their LP relaxations differ.
The tighter the relaxation hugs the integer points, the better the bound, and the less
work a solver needs. A good formulation is one whose relaxation is small.

## The running example

$$
\max\ 2x_1 + 7x_2 \quad\text{s.t.}\quad -5x_1 + 5x_2 \le 14,\quad 7x_1 + 6x_2 \le 36,\quad
0 \le x_1 \le 5,\ 0 \le x_2 \le 6,\quad x \in \mathbb{Z}^2 .
$$

```{python}
#| label: fig-relaxation
#| fig-cap: "The running example. The LP relaxation (red) contains the 17 integer points (dots); its optimum (red star) is $(1.48, 4.28)$ with value $32.9$. The integer hull (green) is the convex hull of the integer points; its best vertex is the integer optimum $(2, 3)$ with value $25$ (green star). Rounding the LP optimum gives $(1, 4)$, which is not even feasible."
G, h = all_rows()
P_lp = polygon(G, h)
pts = integer_points()
hull = convex_hull(pts)
xlp, zlp = lp()
xip, zip_ = ip_optimum()
fig, ax = new_axes(1, xlim=(-0.4, 5.6), ylim=(-0.4, 5.4), size=4.6)
shade_polygon(ax, P_lp, COLORS["weak"], alpha=0.18, label="LP relaxation $P$")
shade_polygon(ax, hull, COLORS["hull"], alpha=0.40, label="integer hull conv$(S)$")
ax.scatter(pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1], s=22, color="black", zorder=4)
mark_point(ax, xlp, COLORS["weak"], marker="*", size=220, label=f"LP optimum, $z = {zlp:.1f}$")
mark_point(ax, xip, COLORS["hull"], marker="*", size=220, label=f"IP optimum, $z = {zip_:.0f}$")
ax.scatter([1], [4], s=70, marker="x", color=COLORS["weak"], zorder=5)
ax.annotate("rounded:\ninfeasible", (1, 4), (0.05, 4.75), fontsize=8.5, color=COLORS["weak"])
# objective direction
d = c / np.linalg.norm(c)
ax.annotate("", xy=(4.3 + 0.8 * d[0], 2.6 + 0.8 * d[1]), xytext=(4.3, 2.6),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", lw=1.6, color="0.3"))
ax.text(4.3, 2.5, "objective", fontsize=8.5, color="0.3", va="top", ha="center")
ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8)
plt.show()
```

The gap between $32.9$ and $25$ is the **integrality gap** of this formulation. Closing
it is what every IP algorithm does, by branching, by cutting, or both.

## The math

Write the integer program as $\max\{c^\top x : x \in S\}$ with
$$
S = P \cap \mathbb{Z}^n, \qquad P = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^n : Ax \le b\}.
$$
A polyhedron $P$ with $P \cap \mathbb{Z}^n = S$ is called a **formulation** of $S$.

### The integer hull

::: {.callout-important}
## Theorem (the integer hull is a polyhedron)
If $A$ and $b$ are rational, then $\operatorname{conv}(S)$, the convex hull of the
integer points of $P$, is a polyhedron. Moreover
$$
\max\{c^\top x : x \in S\} \;=\; \max\{c^\top x : x \in \operatorname{conv}(S)\}
$$
for every $c$, and when the maximum is finite it is attained at a vertex of
$\operatorname{conv}(S)$, which is an integer point.
:::

The polyhedrality statement for general rational data is due to @meyer1974; for a
bounded $P$ it is immediate, since $S$ is finite and the convex hull of finitely many
points is a polytope ([Minkowski–Weyl](../../foundations/polyhedra/minkowski-weyl.qmd)).
The equality holds because a linear function attains the same maximum over a set and
over its convex hull.

So **every integer program is secretly a linear program** over $\operatorname{conv}(S)$.
The catch is that we usually do not know the inequalities describing
$\operatorname{conv}(S)$, and there may be exponentially many of them.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why rationality matters
With irrational data the integer hull need not be a polyhedron. For
$P = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^2_{\ge 0} : x_2 \le \sqrt{2}\, x_1\}$ the integer points come
arbitrarily close to the irrational line, and their convex hull needs infinitely many
inequalities. In practice all data are rational, so this is a theoretical caveat.
:::

### Comparing formulations

For two formulations $P_1, P_2$ of the same $S$, say $P_1$ is **stronger** (tighter) if
$P_1 \subseteq P_2$. Then
$$
z_{\text{IP}} \;\le\; z_{\text{LP}}(P_1) \;\le\; z_{\text{LP}}(P_2)
\qquad\text{for every objective } c,
$$
so the stronger formulation always gives a bound at least as good. The strongest
possible formulation is $\operatorname{conv}(S)$ itself, the **ideal formulation**: its
vertices are integer, so solving the LP relaxation solves the integer program.

```{python}
#| label: fig-nested
#| fig-cap: "Three formulations of the same 17 integer points. Left: the original model. Middle: add the valid inequality $x_2 \\le 3$ (it cuts off no integer point). Right: the ideal formulation, described by $x_1 + x_2 \\le 5$, $-x_1 + x_2 \\le 2$, $x_2 \\le 3$ and $x \\ge 0$. Each is contained in the previous one, and the LP bound falls from 32.9 to 26.1 to the integer optimum 25."
extra2 = [(np.array([0.0, 1.0]), 3.0)]
G2 = np.vstack([G, extra2[0][0]]); h2 = np.append(h, 3.0)
forms = [("original $P$", polygon(G, h), lp()),
         ("$P \\cap \\{x_2 \\leq 3\\}$", polygon(G2, h2), lp(extra=extra2)),
         ("ideal: conv$(S)$", hull, (xip, zip_))]
cols = [COLORS["weak"], COLORS["p2"], COLORS["hull"]]
fig, axes = new_axes(3, xlim=(-0.4, 5.6), ylim=(-0.4, 5.4), size=3.3)
for ax, (name, poly, (xs, zs)), col in zip(axes, forms, cols):
    shade_polygon(ax, P_lp, "#888888", alpha=0.08, lw=0.6)
    shade_polygon(ax, poly, col, alpha=0.35)
    ax.scatter(pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1], s=14, color="black", zorder=4)
    mark_point(ax, xs, col, marker="*", size=170)
    ax.set_title(f"{name}\nLP bound {zs:.1f}", fontsize=10)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

### When the relaxation is automatically ideal

If the constraint matrix $A$ is
[totally unimodular](../../network-optimization/integrality-and-matching/total-unimodularity.qmd)
and $b$ is integer, every vertex of $P$ is integer, so $P = \operatorname{conv}(S)$
[@hoffman1956]. That is why network flow, bipartite matching and assignment problems
never need branching. For a general IP, an ideal formulation can sometimes be built by
adding variables: a description of $\operatorname{conv}(S)$ in a higher-dimensional
space whose projection is the hull. The convex-hull formulation of a disjunction
[@balas1979] is the standard example; see
[Big-M vs. Convex Hull](../disjunctive-programming/big-m-vs-hull.qmd).

## A classic example: facility location

Choose which of $m$ sites to open ($y_i \in \{0,1\}$, fixed cost $f_i$) and assign each
of $n$ customers to an open site ($x_{ij} \ge 0$, cost $c_{ij}$, $\sum_i x_{ij} = 1$).
A customer may only use an open site. Two correct ways to say this:
$$
\text{aggregated:}\quad \sum_{j=1}^n x_{ij} \le n\, y_i \quad (m \text{ constraints}),
\qquad\qquad
\text{disaggregated:}\quad x_{ij} \le y_i \quad (mn \text{ constraints}).
$$
Both have the same integer solutions. But summing the disaggregated constraints over
$j$ gives the aggregated one, so the disaggregated formulation is stronger. In the
aggregated LP relaxation, a site can be "a quarter open" ($y_i = 1/4$) and still serve
two customers fully, paying only a quarter of its fixed cost.

```{python}
#| label: fig-facility
#| fig-cap: "Facility location with 4 candidate sites (squares, fixed costs 25–35) and 8 customers (dots). Left: the aggregated LP relaxation opens every site fractionally (labels show $y_i$) and its bound is about 24% below the true optimum. Right: the disaggregated LP relaxation is already integer: it opens one site, and its bound equals the integer optimum."
res = {k: facility_location(k) for k in (False, True)}
zopt = facility_location(True, integer=True)[0]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.4, 4.0))
for ax, k, title in [(axes[0], False, "aggregated"), (axes[1], True, "disaggregated")]:
    z, y, F, C, X = res[k]
    for i in range(len(F)):
        for j in range(len(C)):
            if X[i, j] > 1e-6:
                ax.plot([F[i, 0], C[j, 0]], [F[i, 1], C[j, 1]], color="0.55",
                        lw=0.6 + 2.2 * X[i, j], zorder=1)
    ax.scatter(C[:, 0], C[:, 1], s=26, color="black", zorder=3)
    for i, (px, py) in enumerate(F):
        col = COLORS["hull"] if y[i] > 0.999 else (COLORS["weak"] if y[i] > 1e-6 else "0.75")
        ax.scatter([px], [py], marker="s", s=110, color=col, edgecolor="white", zorder=4)
        ax.text(px + 0.45, py - 0.35, f"$y={round(abs(y[i]), 3):g}$", ha="left", va="top", fontsize=8.5,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc="white", ec="none", alpha=0.85), zorder=5)
    ax.set_title(f"{title}: LP bound {z:.1f}  (optimum {zopt:.1f})", fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xlim(-0.5, 10.5); ax.set_ylim(-0.5, 10.8); ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The stronger model has more constraints but gives a far better bound, and on large
instances it is usually solved much faster. "Fewer constraints" is not a goal; a small
relaxation is.

## Why it works

Every IP method in the next section works with relaxations:
[branch and bound](../solution-methods/branch-and-bound.qmd) prunes a subproblem when
its relaxation bound cannot beat the best known solution, so better bounds mean more
pruning; [cutting planes](../solution-methods/cutting-planes.qmd) move the formulation
toward $\operatorname{conv}(S)$ while the algorithm runs. A strong formulation gives
both a head start.
